## Overview

This graded assignment consists of creating two Markdown files:

1. One with notes and reflections on what you learned in the course so far.
2. Another that includes Unix shell code.

This assignment revolves around the material for weeks 2 and 3;
the skills you will practice are Markdown, VS Code, and Unix shell basics.

## Detailed steps

### Setting up

- Start a VS Code (`Code Server`) session at OSC OnDemand,
  as we did in class this week,
  selecting the latest available App Code Server version.
  Make sure the VS Code Working Directory is your personal dir,
  `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/<user>`: either set it when you start the session,
  or use the Open Folder functionality once in VS Code.

- In the VS Code file explorer, create a folder `GA1` in your personal dir
  (`/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/<user>/GA1`).
  ***Both files for this assignment should go in this `GA1` folder.***

- I'd recommend creating your two files directly in the file explorer,
  each with a `.md` extension: one for Part A and one for Part B.

### General

Both files should be written in the editor within VS Code,
and I recommend that you keep a **Markdown preview** open to the side while you work,
so you can check that your Markdown renders as you intended.

Include **each** of the following syntax elements at least once
across your two files combined:

| Element             | What it should look like                                                     |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Headers             | Several _header levels_ (`#`, `##`, `###`, ...), used consistently           |
| Bold text           | `**bold**`                                                                   |
| Italic text         | `*italic*` (or `_italic_`)                                                   |
| Inline code         | Single backticks, e.g. for file names and for commands mentioned in a sentence |
| Code blocks         | Triple backticks --- see [Part B](#part-b-a-markdown-document-with-unix-shell-exercises) |
| Unordered list      | Items starting with `-`                                                      |
| Ordered list        | Items starting with `1.`                                                     |
| Hyperlink           | `[link text](url)` or `<url>`                                                |
| Whitespace          | Blank lines between elements, and a space after `#`, `-`, and `1.`           |

: {.striped .hover tbl-colwidths="[22,78]"}

### Part A: A Markdown document with class notes

Write a summary of what you've learned so far in this course.
The summary doesn't need to be comprehensive,
and can focus on a few specific elements you thought were interesting or that
you'd like to summarize.
Make sure to highlight the following
(while also including other things you think are important):

- One or more things you were excited to learn.

- One or more things you are (still) confused about.

- In last week's [Project file organization lecture](../week02/w2a_project-org.qmd),
  you were given a set of recommendations about how to organize your project files
  and document your research.
  Discuss a few of these recommendations:

  - At least one that you think will be really useful.
  - At least one that you are not positive about.
    For example, a recommendation you're not sure you agree with,
    or one you think would in practice be hard to implement in your project(s).

  Include _why_ you think the recommendation will be useful or not useful
  in your specific research context.

### Part B: A Markdown document with Unix shell exercises

Most of the questions below should be answered with Unix shell code
and the output of that code.
A few of them instead (or additionally) ask you to explain, predict,
or reflect on something.

Copy each of the numbered instructions below into your document,
and insert your answers in between ---
with the code and its output each in its own code block:

- **Code** goes in a code block marked as `bash` (```` ```bash ````),
  so that it gets shell syntax highlighting.
- **Output** goes in a code block with no language specified (just ```` ``` ````).
- Every command in your code blocks should have a **comment** above it
  (a line starting with `#`) that briefly says what the command does.
  It's a good habit to comment your code.

_It does not matter what your working dir is when you start working on this._

::: callout-tip

## Solutions

Part A doesn't have a single correct answer, so below are solutions to Part B only.
In the example output, paths and node names will differ from yours:
`<user>` stands for your user name.

### Part B

<details><summary>**1.** Print the location of your Home dir using a path shortcut.</summary>

The `~` path shortcut points to your Home dir:

```bash
# Print the path to my Home dir
echo ~
```
```bash-out
/users/PAS3493/<user>
```

- The project ID in your path may differ (e.g. `PAS0471`).
- Alternatively, you could have moved to your Home dir with `cd ~` and then run `pwd`.
- Note that `echo $HOME` prints the same path, but `$HOME` is an _environment variable_
  rather than a path shortcut.

</details>

<details><summary>**2.** Navigate to your Home dir using an environment variable.</summary>

```bash
# Move to my Home dir
cd $HOME
```

This command doesn't print any output,
though you could run `pwd` afterwards to confirm where you are.
Note that `cd ~` and `cd` without an argument would also take you to your Home dir,
but neither uses an environment variable.

</details>

<details><summary>**3.** Relative or absolute path?</summary>

This was an **absolute** path:
the shell replaces `$HOME` by the full path to your Home dir
(`/users/PAS3493/<user>`), which starts with the root dir `/`.
As a result, `cd $HOME` works regardless of what your working dir is.

</details>

<details><summary>**4.** Navigate from your Home dir to `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER` using a relative path.</summary>

```bash
# Move up three levels to the root dir, then down to my personal dir
cd ../../../fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER
```

- Your Home dir `/users/PAS3493/<user>` is three levels below the root dir `/`,
  so you need three `..` to get there.
- Typing out your user name instead of using `$USER` is fine too.
- Any path starting with `/` or `~` is _not_ a relative path.

</details>

<details><summary>**5.** Absolute path with <kbd>Tab</kbd> completion.</summary>

```bash
# Go back to my Home dir
cd ~

# Move to my personal dir with an absolute path
cd /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/<user>
```

<kbd>Tab</kbd> can't complete (all of) a name when multiple entries
start with what you have typed so far:

- **After `/fs/ess/P`** (or `/fs/ess/PAS`):
  there are many project dirs starting with `PAS`,
  so you need to type (most of) `3493` before <kbd>Tab</kbd> can finish it.
- **Within your user name**: other users' dirs in `people`
  may start with the same letter(s) as yours.
  How many characters you had to type therefore depends on your user name ---
  just enough to distinguish it from all others in `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people`.

</details>

<details><summary>**6.** Typing <kbd>"</kbd> and pressing <kbd>Enter</kbd>.</summary>

- **What**: The prompt is replaced by a `>` on the next line, and nothing is executed.
- **Why**: The command is incomplete: the shell is waiting for the closing `"`.
- **How to get out**: Press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>C</kbd> to get your regular prompt back.
  (Typing a closing `"` and pressing <kbd>Enter</kbd> also gets you out,
  but produces an error, since `""` is not a valid command.)

</details>

<details><summary>**7.** Pasting together long-form options.</summary>

```bash
# Try to paste together two long-form options
cal --julian--three
```
```bash-out
cal: unrecognized option '--julian--three'
Try 'cal --help' for more information.
```

**No**, long-form options can't be pasted together:
the result is interpreted as a single (non-existing) long option.
Each long option needs its own `--`, as in `cal --julian --three`.

</details>

<details><summary>**8.** Julian calendar for the month and year of your birth.</summary>

For example, for July 1990:

```bash
# Print a Julian calendar for July 1990
cal -j 7 1990
```
```bash-out
          July 1990
Sun Mon Tue Wed Thu Fri Sat
182 183 184 185 186 187 188
189 190 191 192 193 194 195
196 197 198 199 200 201 202
203 204 205 206 207 208 209
210 211 212
```

- In this example, July 15th, 1990 is day **196**.
- `cal -j july 1990` and `cal --julian 7 1990` also work.
  You can even include the day, as in `cal -j 15 7 1990`,
  which will highlight that day in the output.
- The order of the arguments matters: the month comes before the year,
  so `cal -j 1990 7` gives an error.

</details>

<details><summary>**9.** Login node or compute node?</summary>

- You are on a **compute node**: you started VS Code (Code Server) as
  an OnDemand Interactive App, and these always run on compute nodes.
  (Another clue: the node name in your prompt, e.g. `p0133`, is not a login node name.)

- Print the node name:

  ```bash
  # Print the name of the node I'm working on
  echo $HOSTNAME
  ```
  ```bash-out
  p0133.ten.osc.edu
  ```

  Your node name will differ: Pitzer compute node names start with a `p`
  followed by digits, whereas login node names look like `pitzer-login01`.

</details>
